name: Summer Vacation
description: While reading the statement of this problem, we recommend forgetting that summer consists of $$$92$$$ days and that a day consists of $$$1440$$$ minutes. This is Berland, and things are different here. Monocarp is a student at a provincial university in Berland. The summer holidays have just begun, and they will last for the next $$$n$$$ days. Monocarp has long dreamed of going to the capital of Berland, so he will choose one day $$$i$$$ among these days, arrive in the capital on that day, and spend the rest of the holidays there. The capital of Berland is not a very cheap city, and Monocarp has $$$0$$$ Berland dollars with him. Naturally, this is not enough to visit interesting places and buy souvenirs. Therefore, on some days in the capital, Monocarp will work as a freelancer. He does not want to work in his hometown, since he has already spent the whole academic year doing university assignments. Formally, on the $$$i$$$-th day of the holidays, Monocarp will have $$$a_i$$$ free minutes, which he will spend either working or resting and buying souvenirs. If Monocarp has at least $$$a_i$$$ dollars at the beginning of the $$$i$$$-th day, then on that day he will spend them on rest and souvenirs at a rate of $$$1$$$ dollar per minute; that is, during this day, he will spend $$$a_i$$$ dollars. Otherwise, he will spend this time working, earning $$$1$$$ dollar per minute; that is, during this day, he will earn $$$a_i$$$ dollars. Note that Monocarp always makes his decision for the entire day; it is impossible for him to both spend and earn money during the same day. Your task is to determine, for each number of days $$$k$$$ from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, how many dollars Monocarp will have left after the last day of the holidays if he lives in the capital for exactly $$$k$$$ last days (i. e. if he arrives on the day $$$(n-k+1)$$$).
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^{5}$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_{i}$$$ ($$$1 \le a_{i} \le n$$$).
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ integers, where the $$$k$$$-th integer must be equal to the number of dollars Monocarp will have left if he lives in the capital for exactly $$$k$$$ last days (i. e. if he arrives on the day $$$(n-k+1)$$$).
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2242F — Summer Vacation [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
